stops.name: Portovenere, Abul-Abbas the elephant lands in Italy
stops.campa: Isaac the Jew, sent four years before as the emperor's envoy to Harun al-Rashid, king of the Persians, returns out of Africa with the caliph's gift walking behind him: an elephant. The beast has come from Baghdad to the coast, over the sea in a ship built or found to bear him, and in October he steps ashore at Portovenere on the Ligurian rock. Italy has not seen his kind since the triumphs of Rome. Children run from the harbor to touch and flee; the mountains stand between the elephant and his emperor, and the snow is already on the passes.

stops.name: Vercelli, the elephant winters below the Alps
stops.campa: The Alps cannot be crossed; the snow lies deep on the Mont Cenis where armies passed in autumn, and an elephant is not an army. So Isaac and Abul-Abbas turn into winter quarters at Vercelli in the rice-flat plain of the Po, and a Lombard town spends a winter feeding, stabling and marveling at a beast out of the book of Maccabees. Hay is requisitioned; a barn is a palace. In the spring, says the annalist with perfect calm, they will walk over the mountains. The elephant waits out the snow like a patient ambassador, which is what he is.
stops.quote: Because he could not cross the Alps on account of the snow, he wintered at Vercelli.

stops.name: Aachen, the missi ride out; the empire ordered
stops.campa: In this year the emperor reorganizes the realm as a man reorders his house: the great capitulary goes out, and pairs of missi dominici, one count, one bishop, the emperor's eyes doubled, ride circuits into every province to hear the widow and the orphan, to correct the judges, to take from every free man above twelve a new oath to Charles as emperor. Law is written down for Saxon and Frisian and Lombard alike; the survey-takers count and record. The empire becomes a thing of parchment as much as of swords, riders on all roads, carrying the emperor's justice in saddlebags.
stops.quote: The most serene and most Christian lord emperor Charles has chosen from his nobles the wisest and most prudent men... and sent them through his whole kingdom.

stops.name: Aachen, the elephant delivered to the emperor
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July Isaac comes up the road to Aachen with the elephant and all the gifts of the king of the Persians, and delivers everything to the emperor in his palace. The annalist gives the beast a full sentence and his name: the elephant's name was Abul Abaz. The gray mountain kneels in the palace yard; the court of the Franks stands in a ring, utterly silenced. Baghdad has bowed to Aachen in the most magnificent way one empire can bow to another: by sending it a living wonder. He will live at the emperor's side eight years.
stops.quote: The name of the elephant was Abul Abaz.

stops.name: Thionville, the ordering of the succession
stops.campa: At the winter palace of Thionville on the Moselle the emperor gathers the magnates and divides the future: the Divisio Regnorum, sealed the sixth of February, parts the empire among the three sons of Hildegard, Charles the eldest to Francia, Pippin to Italy, Louis to Aquitaine, with careful clauses for peace between brothers and none at all for the imperial title, which the emperor keeps folded in God's hand. Copies go to Rome for the pope's subscription. It is prudent, paternal, complete. And heaven will annul it clause by clause, taking the sons before the father.

stops.name: Aachen, the water-clock of brass strikes the hours
stops.campa: New envoys of Harun al-Rashid reach the court bearing, among silks, perfumes and a pavilion-tent of marvelous size, a clock of brass driven by water: at each hour the number of bronze balls falls ringing on a cymbal beneath, and twelve horsemen ride out of twelve doors, shutting behind them the windows that stood open. The Franks crowd the machine to watch time itself perform. It is the East's second great sermon to the West (first a beast, now an engine), and the annalist describes its workings with the wonder of a man describing an angel's anatomy.
stops.quote: A clock of brass, a marvelous mechanical contraption, in which the course of the twelve hours moved according to a water clock... and twelve horsemen who at the end of each hour stepped out of twelve windows, closing the previously open windows by their movements.

stops.name: Milan, Pippin the son dies
stops.campa: Pippin, king of Italy, the emperor's second son, the boy who broke into the Avar Ring, the king who warred on Venice in her lagoons, dies of sickness in Italy on the eighth of July, thirty-three years old, and is buried at Milan in Sant'Ambrogio. The Divisio of Thionville loses its southern third; a bastard grandson, Bernard, will be set over Italy in his place. The emperor is on the Danish war when the news rides north. The canon begins here the drumbeat of the griefs: heaven is emptying the emperor's table one seat at a time.

stops.name: Lippeham on the Rhine, the death of Abul-Abbas
stops.campa: Godofrid king of the Danes has harried Frisia with two hundred ships, and the emperor, past sixty, calls out the host and takes the elephant on campaign, the living standard of the empire marching against the north. At Lippeham, where the Lippe meets the Rhine, the army waits on the muster; and there Abul-Abbas, nine years a Frank, dies suddenly. The annalist gives him a death-notice among kings and battles, without apology. The emperor has lost, in one summer, a son and an elephant, and the canon records both griefs in the same annal-year, side by side.
stops.quote: There the elephant which Aaron, the king of the Saracens, had sent him, died a sudden death.

stops.name: The camp on the Danish march, the fireball throws the emperor from his horse
stops.campa: On this same last Saxon campaign, riding out of camp before daybreak, the emperor sees a ball of fire fall suddenly across the clear sky, blazing from right to left through the darkness. As all men stare, his horse drops headlong and throws him so hard against the ground that the clasp of his cloak snaps and his sword-belt is torn from him; the attendants who run to him must unarm the emperor of the West where he lies in the dirt. The javelin in his fist is flung twenty feet clear. The register does not soften it: heaven has begun addressing him directly.
stops.quote: Charles himself saw a ball of fire fall suddenly from the heavens with a great light, just as he was leaving camp before sunrise to set out on the march... the horse which he was riding gave a sudden plunge, head foremost, and fell, and threw him to the ground so heavily that his cloak buckle was broken and his sword belt shattered.

stops.name: Aachen, the death of Charles the Younger; the emperor weeps
stops.campa: On the fourth of December dies Charles the Younger, the eldest, the soldier-son shaped in his father's image, heir of Francia and of the great name, unmarried, childless, suddenly, of a stroke. Of the three kings among whom Thionville parted the world, only Louis of Aquitaine is left alive. Einhard, who watched, wrote that the emperor bore the deaths of his sons and of his daughter Rotrud with less patience than his greatness of soul had promised: his affection mastered him, and he wept. The strongest man of the age sits in the octagon's gallery and cries like any father, and the canon honors him for it.
stops.quote: When his sons and his daughter died, he was not so calm as might have been expected from his remarkably strong mind, for his affections were no less strong, and moved him to tears.

stops.name: Mainz, the bridge of ten years burns in three hours
stops.campa: The wooden bridge at Mainz, five hundred paces over the Rhine, ten years in the building, the emperor's proudest work of peace, which he meant one day to remake in stone, catches fire and is so utterly consumed in three hours that not one splinter remains above the waterline. The river carries off the charcoal of a decade. Einhard sets it first among the portents of the end: the works of the reign have begun to be recalled, as a lord recalls his loans. The emperor, they say, receives the news in silence.
stops.quote: The wooden bridge over the Rhine at Mayence... was so completely consumed in three hours by an accidental fire that not a single splinter of it was left, except what was under water.

stops.name: Aachen, the portico falls; the word PRINCEPS fades from the wall
stops.campa: The omens gather at Aachen itself. On Ascension Day the gallery between basilica and palace, built with such pains, falls suddenly in ruins to the ground. The sun and moon are repeatedly darkened; a black spot sits on the sun for seven days. Lightning strikes the chapel and the gilded apple falls from the roof-ridge. And in the red-painted inscription that rings the dome, between BASILICA and the name of God, the word PRINCEPS, Karolus Princeps, fades letter by letter until, months before the end, it cannot be read at all. He says he takes no account of such things. He orders nothing repainted.
stops.quote: The letters of the word Princeps were so effaced as to be no longer decipherable... But Charles despised, or affected to despise, all these omens, as having no reference whatever to him.
